newsitem.title: UK: INSIGHT-Coffee due $200 down, may stop at $50-$70.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Coffee due $200 down, may stop at $50-$70.

text.p: SEPT Close * Support * Resist * RSI14 * MA10 * MA40
Coffee futures were due to open $200 down on paper on Thursday after a lower close in New York on Wednesday. But traders said in practice, it could do $50-$70 lower.
Chartwise, the market is attempting to build a base at above $1,500 before moving higher again, analysts said.
New York arabica futures shed steep early gains to finish lower in volatile trading on Wednesday, pressured by eleventh-hour speculative liquidation.
Prices were higher from the start as speculators bought amid extended forecasts calling for colder weather in Brazil and continued concerns about tight prompt supply.
The spot September contract rallied to 198.00 cents per lb -- its highest level in more than six weeks. It ended 3.15 down at 185.75.
Traders said long-term Brazilian weather outlooks predicting colder temperatures in the coffee belt during the weekend of August 9 set a bullish tone.
The robusta futures in London pared most early losses as New York moved higher to end slightly steadier.
Analysts said the sharply lower call this morning would help the market fill a downside chart gap at between $1,615 and $1,640 -- seen as the initial support. The next support is seen at $1,600.
But bigger support was seen at $1,550 and then $1,500.
"I think the market is attempting to build a base at above $1,500 and I think in time it will certainly push the market higher," said Adrian Haylor, an analyst at Sucden.
The spot July contract goes off the board at lunchtime on Thursday.

In other news, Brazil's soluble coffee industry wants to import robusta coffee to alleviate a supply shortage but has agreed to a government request to wait a little longer, an industry spokesman said.
Elsewhere, fast-food chain McDonald's Corp is drawing up plans to supply all its restaurants worldwide with Colombian coffee, company sources said.
"This is a plan we're working on in conjunction with Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation," Andres Munoz, head of marketing for McDonald's Colombian operations, told Reuters.
Currently, McDonald's uses coffee from a variety of countries purchased in international markets.
